html:
A gathering of Theravada Buddhist monks held in Mandalay, Burma, in 1871 under King Mindon, to recite and check the whole Pali canon. Burmese count it as the fifth great council since the Buddha's time.

Mindon ruled what was left of the Konbaung kingdom after Britain took Lower Burma in 1852. He founded Mandalay as a new royal capital and set out to make it a centre of Buddhist learning, partly to show that the faith was safe under a Burmese king. Some 2,400 monks, led by three senior elders, recited the texts over five months.

The checked text had already been carved in Pali on 729 marble slabs, each in its own small shrine at the Kuthodaw Pagoda at the foot of Mandalay Hill. It is often called the world's largest book. The council looked back to the writing down of the Pali canon in Sri Lanka two thousand years earlier. Fourteen years later, in 1885, the British took the rest of Burma. A sixth council met in Rangoon from 1954 to 1956.
